Adler, Grossman, Kezwer, Rapp and Young v.

The Queen in right of Ontario,

the Minister of Education and the Minister of Health

Elgersma, Pott, Dostal, Fernhout and Ontario Alliance

of Christian School Societies v.

Attorney General for Ontario,

the Minister of Education and the Minister of Health

[Indexed as: Adler v. Ontario]

9 O.R. (3d) 676

[1992] O.J. No. 1628

Action No. RE 1854/91Q and RE 183/92

Ontario Court (General Division),

Anderson J.

August 4, 1992

Charter of Rights
and Freedoms -- Freedom of religion --
Non- funding of Jewish and independent Christian schools by Province of Ontario
violating
s. 2(a)
of Charter -- Violation justified under
s. 1
of Charter --
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1, 2(a) --
Education Act, R.S.O.
1990, c. E.2
.

Charter of Rights
and Freedoms -- Equality rights -- Non- funding of Jewish
and independent Christian schools by Province of Ontario violating
s. 15
of
Charter -- Violation justified under
s. 1
of Charter -- Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms, ss. 1, 15 --
Education Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2
.

In two separate applications, the applicants sought declarations that the
non-funding of, in one case, Jewish day school education and, in the other
case, independent Christian schools in Ontario infringed the applicants' rights
under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. They sought other related
relief, including a declaration that they were entitled to the benefit of
funding by the Province of Ontario on a basis equivalent to the funding
provided to Roman Catholic separate schools and to public schools.

Held, the applications should be dismissed.

Funding of Roman Catholic separate schools was not a relevant consideration
in determining the rights of these applicants. While the issues raised in these
cases had not been rendered res judicata by the upholding of the
constitutionality of Roman Catholic funding by the Bill 30 Reference (that
constitutional reference not having involved a lis inter partes), legislation
which has been held to be a valid exercise of the provincial power to legislate
in matters pertaining to education cannot, at the same time, provide the
fulcrum for an argument that it is unconstitutional in its effect. The question
put to the court in the Bill 30 Reference was framed in terms such as to invite
full scrutiny under the
Charter
and the court dealt with it accordingly. The
funding of Roman Catholic separate schools in Ontario is a constitutional
anomaly, with its roots in a historic political compromise made as an incident
of the Confederation of 1867.

The applicants' rights under
s. 15
of the
Charter
were infringed. The

Education Act
created a distinction which resulted in a violation of the
applicants' right to equal benefit of the law. Those whose children attend
public schools receive the benefit of an education for their children free of
any direct costs attributable to that education. Those whose children do not
attend public schools, because their religious convictions prevent them from
allowing their children to do so, do not receive that benefit. This distinction
is based on religion.

The applicants' freedom of religion guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
was
also infringed. The
Education Act
makes school attendance mandatory, and the
price of escape from that mandatory provision is the payment of tuition fees by
those parents who, by religious and conscientious belief, are precluded from
taking advantage of the publicly funded school system. The legislation imposed
a cost or burden on the applicants in securing for their children education
consistent with their religious beliefs.

The impugned legislation was saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
. The legislative
objectives, which included the provision of a tuition-free, secular, public
education universally accessible to all Ontario residents, and the
establishment of a public education system which fosters and promotes the
values of a pluralist, democratic society, were of sufficient importance to
warrant overriding a constitutionally protected right or freedom. There was a
rational connection between the objectives and the means chosen to achieve
those objectives. The scheme envisaged by the
Education Act
impaired as little
as possible the right of freedom of religion and equality. The question of
whether the means chosen to give effect to the objective were proportionate to
the adverse effects on the applicants was largely one of opinion. The objective
of a broadly based system of secular public education is a complex and onerous
undertaking. That some elements of the population would be in some way and to
some extent offended and inconvenienced was almost inevitable. Having regard
for those considerations, the effects were not out of proportion to the
objective.

APPLICATIONS for declaration that non-funding by the Province of Ontario of
Jewish and independent schools violates the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
. (For related proceedings, see (1992),
1992 CanLII 7415 (ON CTGD)
, 8 O.R. (3d) 200, 88 D.L.R.
(4th) 632 (Gen. Div.).)

ANDERSON J.:--

I. NATURE OF PROCEEDINGS AND IDENTITY OF PARTIES

The first of these applications will be referred to throughout these reasons
as the "Adler application" and the applicants collectively as the
"Adler applicants", save where the context otherwise requires.
Similarly, the second action will be referred to as the "Elgersma
application" and the applicants will be referred to as the "Elgersma
applicants", save where the context otherwise requires. The Adler
applicants seek, along with other relief, a declaration that the non- funding
of Jewish day school education in Ontario is unconstitutional. The further
relief sought by the Adler applicants will be set out with more particularity
in a subsequent portion of these reasons. The Elgersma applicants seek, along
with other relief, a declaration that the non- funding of independent Christian
schools, which are members of the Ontario Alliance of Christian School
Societies, infringes rights of the applicants guaranteed under the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The additional relief sought in the Elgersma
application will also be set out subsequently.

At an early stage in these proceedings, several parties moved to intervene.
In the result, intervener status was granted to the Ontario Federation of
Independent Schools (OFIS), the Metropolitan Toronto School Board (MTSB), and
the Ontario School Boards Association (OPSBA) and the Canadian Civil Liberties
Association (CCLA). On the argument of the substantive applications, the OFIS
supported the applicants and MTSB and OSBA supported the respondents.

(
1
) The Adler application

This is an application by five parents of children in Jewish day schools.
Full-time Jewish day schools have existed in Ontario since 1949. There are now
25 such schools in the province, of which 19 are in Metropolitan Toronto, two
in Hamilton, two in Ottawa (one of which is a French language school), one in
London, and one in Kitchener. Approximately 10,000 students attend these
schools. The schools provide secular educational studies for approximately half
the school day, and Jewish religious instruction and Judaic studies for the
other half. The school day is typically an hour or more longer than in the
public schools, so that the extra religious education is not provided at the
expense of the general studies program. The secular portion of the curriculum
in Ontario's Jewish day schools conforms to current Ministry of Education
guidelines and requirements, both at the elementary and high school levels.
Students receive recognized high school diplomas at the end of their studies,
and at any stage in their schooling they can transfer easily into the public
education system. Virtually every teacher in the Jewish day schools holds
either a certificate from the Ontario Ministry of Education or from another jurisdiction
in Canada or the United States. There is no discrimination in hiring practices.
There are many non- Jewish teachers teaching the general studies portion of the
curriculum; teachers of the religious studies portion are of the Jewish faith,
which has been accepted as a bona fide occupational qualification.

Each of the Adler applicants has testified to his or her belief that the
Jewish education necessary for the practice of the Jewish religion can only be
achieved in a Jewish day school environment. It is not and cannot be expected
to be available in the public system. I accept their evidence. There is also
expert evidence which I accept that the Jewish community's survival as an
identifiable and practising religious community depends upon broad access for
Jewish children to Jewish day schools.

Such schools receive no direct funding from the government of Ontario. Their
funding is received from the parents of the children attending, who pay tuition
fees, from monies raised by the schools themselves, and by various activities
of the Jewish community. The cost per child ranges from $5,000 in some schools
to a high of $7,800 for high school. Parents pay tuition fees which account, on
average, for 77 per cent of the cost of elementary school education (Grades
1-8) and 51 per cent of high school education. By way of contrast, a contrast
which is fundamental to these proceedings, both the public schools of the
province and the Roman Catholic separate schools are fully supported by a
complex arrangement of property taxes and provincial grants.

The relief sought by the Adler applicants is outlined in the application in
the following terms:

(1) A declaration that the non-funding of Jewish day school education in
Ontario is unconstitutional;

(
2
) A declaration that the Applicants and the parents or families of
children in Jewish day schools in Ontario are entitled to the benefit of
funding by the Province of Ontario on a basis equivalent to the funding
provided to Roman Catholic separate schools and to public schools;

(
3
) An order that the Province of Ontario provide funds to the Applicants
and to all parents or families of children in Jewish day schools in Ontario, by
means of a per capita grant system or other system of funding based on the
student population of those schools;

(
4
) In the alternative to (3) above, an order that the Province of Ontario
provide funds to the Applicants and to all parents or families of children in
Jewish day schools in Ontario, by means of a per capita grant or other system
of funding to cover the secular portion of the education provided in those
schools;

(
5
) An order that the Province of Ontario extend school health support
services to the children in the Jewish day schools . . .

(The fifth head of relief relating to school health support services lends
itself to consideration separate from that sought in the first four
paragraphs.) In the factum filed on their behalf, the order requested by the
Adler applicants is outlined in the following terms:

66. The Applicants therefore respectfully request that the Court declare the
non-funding of Jewish day schools unconstitutional, that it state the
principles by which the Jewish day schools and other religious-based schools
must be funded in the Province of Ontario, and that it direct the Ontario
Government to implement such principles by authorizing the funding of these
schools and by extending health services to these schools as well.

(2) The Elgersma application

The Ontario Alliance of Christian School Societies (OACSS) is a non-profit
corporation which has been active since 1952 in the promotion of Christian
elementary and secondary education. It is a federation of Christian school
societies, the majority of which operate elementary or secondary Christian
schools. There are currently 74 member Christian school societies which operate
75 schools -- 73 in Ontario and two in the Maritimes. Eleven of the 75 schools
are secondary schools, all of which are located in Ontario. In the 1991-92 school
year, 11,614 students were enrolled in OACSS schools in Ontario, almost 2,000
of whom are enrolled in secondary schools. Membership in OACSS is open to any
incorporated, non-profit society whose purpose is to provide to children a
Christian education in the Calvinistic or Reformed Christian tradition. Member
school societies must adopt guidelines set out by OACSS. Membership in each
individual school society is open to all active, adult Christian church members
who assent to the society's aims and confessional principles, who pay the
prescribed membership fee, and who indicate a willingness to be actively
involved in the work of the society. Most society members are members of the
Christian Reformed Church.

The religious philosophy of education which imbues OACSS member schools was
summarized in the judgment of Mr. Justice Muldoon in R. v. McBurney,
1984 CanLII 5806 (FC)
, 84 D.T.C.
6494, 19 E.T.R. 15 (F.C.T.D.), at pp. 6495, 6498-99 D.T.C., pp. 17-18, 23, 25
E.T.R., as follows:

. . . the public schools providing a necessarily secular education, do not
impart that hour-by-hour, subject-by- subject infusion of Christian values and
interpretation of subject matter which the plaintiff and his fellows seek for
their children's education. Neither do the Roman Catholic Separate Schools. . .
.

Studies of the Bible and of the Christian religion are not merely core
subjects of schools, because, transcending the teaching of particular subjects,
Christian thought, perceptions values and works permeate the entire educational
formation the young people who are enrolled in those schools. The charitable
quality of the schools operated by the three non-profit corporations could well
be characterized as both educational and religious. . . . . .

Read in light of each corporation's constitution, the respective curricula
demonstrate, as the witnesses testified, that the subjects offered are taught
as vehicles for the expression and inculcation of religious faith. . . . . . .
. .

All three witnesses testified clearly, as was amply confirmed on cross-examination,
that the curricula include, and the schools present and teach secular subjects,
to be sure. But it is also clear that religious teaching was and is not kept
separate and apart from the teaching of secular subjects. It was and is blended
with them such that, if the secular and religious teachings were (to make an
analogy) chemical elements, they would be combined in solution of varying
proportions from hour to hour throughout the school year. There is no doubt
that the enrolled children were and are being provided with knowledge and being
taught skills which will serve them well in secular society. There is equally
no doubt that at all material times they were simultaneously being instructed
and edified in Christian precepts, and that the teaching of secular subjects
was utilized to that end.

The Christian Reformed Church has pronounced on the central role played by
education in the development of a Christian. The constitution of the church,
the Church Order of the Christian Reformed Church, stipulates (in Article 71)
that:

The Consistory shall diligently encourage members of the congregation to
establish and maintain good Christian schools, and shall urge parents to have
their children instructed in the schools according to the demands of the
covenant.

Two major church synodical pronouncements have interpreted this fundamental
obligation of parents (Acts of Synod, 1898):

Not a general, but a specifically Reformed instruction is the requirement
for our children. Indeed, no educational system is satisfactory, but the
acknowledgment of the necessity of regeneration and additionally the
acknowledgment of the covenant relationship in which God has placed our
children, are the principles from which education must proceed.

Christian education according to Reformed principles is the incontrovertible
duty of Reformed Christians. All ministers and elders must labour to the utmost
of their power in the promotion of Christian education wherever and whenever
possible.

and (Acts of Synod, 1955):

The responsibility for education rests upon the parents. Parents have the
right and duty to avail themselves of assistance of social institutions which
are able and willing to carry forward their God given tasks. To entrust their
children's education to agencies that violate their divinely ordained task
represents, on the part of parents, a flagrant violation of their stewardship.

Each of the individual applicants deposed to their belief that their
religion imposes upon them a duty as parents to ensure that their children are
educated in a Christian environment. The sincerity of these beliefs is not in
issue.

OACSS member schools do not receive government funding. In the 1990-91
school year, member schools obtained funds for operation from the following
sources: 70 per cent from parental tuition pledges, 21 per cent from community
donations and 9 per cent from miscellaneous fund-raising activities. Tuition
pledges for member schools are set on a per family, rather than a per student,
basis. Sixty per cent of member schools request fixed annual tuition pledges
ranging from $3,000 to $6,000 while the remaining school societies request
tuition pledges geared to a range of family incomes: from a minimum of $2,500
for yearly income below $25,000 to a maximum of $6,000 for incomes above
$60,000. All member school societies have student assistance funds to help
needy families who cannot pay the entire tuition.

The relief sought in the Elgersma application is set out in the notice of
application in the following terms:

(1) a declaration that the non-funding by the Minister of Education of
independent Christian schools which are members of the Ontario Alliance of
Christian School Societies infringes rights of the applicants guaranteed under

sections 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
;

(2) a declaration that the Applicants, and parents or families of children
in independent Christian schools which are members of the Ontario Alliance of
Christian School Societies, are equally entitled to the benefit of educational
funding by the Province of Ontario as are parents or families of children in
public schools and Roman Catholic separate schools;

(3) an order that the Province of Ontario provide funds to the Applicants
and to all parents or families of children in independent Christian schools
which are members of the Ontario Alliance of Christian School Societies by
means of a per capita grant system or other system of funding based on the
student population of those schools;

(4) a declaration that s. 1 of the Ontario Regulation 638/ 84 (s. 44a of
Reg. 452, R.R.O. 1980, as amended) made under the Health Insurance Act
infringes rights guaranteed under
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
by reason of its failure to provide school health support
services to students in OACSS member schools who require such services and an
order that the Province of Ontario extend school health support services to any
student enrolled in an OACSS member school who requires such services;

(3) The interveners

(a) The Ontario Federation of Independent Schools

OFIS intervenes as a friend of the court in support of the applicants in
each of the two applications.

OFIS is a non-share corporation under the laws of Ontario which exists to
represent, further, and promote the educational and financial interests of
alternative independent schools in the Province of Ontario, in particular, and
to promote the prior right of parents to choose the kind of education that
should be given to their children generally. It represents approximately 114
independent schools in Ontario, having a total enrolment of approximately 7,000
students. It represents an association of religious schools of several
denominations. While a substantial number of the schools which OFIS represents
have been established for specific religious purposes and aim their program to
instil religious values and beliefs, other member schools have as their
explicit purpose a fostering and instilling of values and beliefs not
specifically linked to any form of religion, but emphasizing certain
pedagogical values and goals. Its position on these applications as outlined in
the factum filed by its counsel is in the following terms:

2. OFIS does not rely on the existence of public funding for Ontario Roman
Catholic Separate Schools in support of its contention that the Applicants'
rights under the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
("Charter")
are infringed by the existing system of providing public funding for Ontario
schools.

3. OFIS instead asserts that the practice of granting public support for the
education of children attending Ontario Public Schools, in the absence of
equivalent funding for the Applicants' children, infringes
Sections 2
,
7
and

15(1)
of the
Charter
and that such infringements are unjustifiable in a free
and democratic society.

4. OFIS takes no position on the manner in which the Crown in Right of
Ontario should organize public funding for Ontario schools in order to comply
with its
Charter
obligations; rather, OFIS contends that however educational
funding in Ontario is organized, funding must support the education of the
Applicants' children on a basis equivalent to the support given to the
education of children attending Ontario Public Schools.

(b) The Metropolitan Toronto School Board and Ontario Public School Boards
Association

MTSB is a corporation continued under
s. 133(1)
of the
Municipality of
Metropolitan Toronto Act , R.S.O. 1990, c. M.62
. Its statutory duties and
powers include the compiling of proposals and budgets for public school
education for Metropolitan Toronto, as well as the receipt and distribution of
all funding for public school education, both from legislative grants, if any,
and from local taxation rates, with respect to six area boards of education and
the French-Language School Council.

OPSBA is an association of public boards of education created in 1989 from a
merger of three organizations, namely, the Association of Large School Boards
of Ontario, the Northern Ontario School Trustees Association, and the Ontario
Public School Trustees Association. OPSBA is the only association of public
school boards in Ontario. It represents over 90 constituent public school
boards which are responsible for the education of over one million children.
OPSBA is principally involved in the co-ordination of policies and practices of
common concern among its member boards for the provision of public education in
Ontario. As such, it is a primary advocate of the interests of public education
in the province.

These interveners filed a joint factum and were represented on the hearing
of the applications by the same counsel. Where subsequent reference is made to
them, it may be taken that a reference to MTSB includes both of these
interveners, unless the context indicates otherwise. These interveners support
the respondents in asking that the applications be dismissed.

(c) Canadian Civil Liberties Association

CCLA is a national organization created in 1964. According to material filed
in support of its motion to intervene, it has more than 7,000 individual
members, eight affiliated chapters across the country, and more than 50
associated group members which themselves represent additional persons. It was
incorporated to promote the respect for, and observance of, fundamental human
rights and civil liberties, and to defend, extend and foster their recognition.
Its objectives include a promotion of individual equality before and under the
law, and the protection of fundamental rights and liberties, such as freedom of
conscience and religion. It supports non- denominational public schools and
entertains the view that such schools provide an opportunity for various
religious groups to develop appreciation and respect for each other, and that
such tolerance will, in turn, foster religious freedom.

It supported the respondents in asking that the applications be dismissed.

II. RELEVANT CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS
