III. FUNDING OF PUBLIC SCHOOLS AND ROMAN CATHOLIC SEPARATE SCHOOLS

School board expenditures are funded from two sources: provincial grants and
property taxes. The Ministry of Education provides financial assistance to the
school boards in the form of a grant. The amount of grant paid is the
difference between the total amount recognized for grant purposes and the
amount raised locally by applying a provincially uniform mill rate to
assessment of the property designed to support a given school board. This
funding model applies to both the public school and the separate school system.
Both the property taxes raised by the local boards and the provincial grants
paid to local school boards vary from school board to school board, depending
on a number of variables. No tuition fees are payable by students attending
these schools. As already indicated, such funding is not available to Jewish
parochial schools nor to the schools such as are represented by OACSS. It is in
the funding provided to public and Roman Catholic separate schools and the
absence of such funding for Jewish parochial schools and schools such as are
represented by OACSS that the constitutional infringements alleged by the
applicants have their genesis.

In my deliberations following the argument, and in the formulation of these
reasons, I have become conscious of the need for a compendious term to describe
schools of the kind with which the applicants are concerned. "Private
school" has implications, in common parlance, which are not appropriate,
and in the context of this case is, in a measure, contentious. "Independent
school" has an ambit larger than the applicants' range of interest. I have
decided, however, on "independent school". I recognize that its
implications are wider than the range of interests which directly concern the
applicants, but with the background here given, I trust it may serve.

IV. OUTLINE OF THE APPLICANTS' CLAIMS

Reduced to their narrowest compass, and unembellished by the abstract
concepts, voluminous exposition, and ornate language, which seem to
characterize constitutional arguments and their disposition, the applicants'
complaint is along these lines. School attendance is mandatory and parents are
under a statutory obligation to cause children to attend school. These
requirements can be met by attendance at a public school or a Roman Catholic
separate school. Such attendance does not require the payment of any fees by
the parents. The applicants are precluded by the dictates of conscience and
religion from sending their children to either of these schools. They are
required therefore to provide satisfactory instruction for their children
elsewhere. This entails sending them to independent schools at which the
parents must pay the tuition fees. Thus they do not receive equal benefit of
the law as required by
s. 15
of the
Charter
, and there is interference with
their rights of religion and conscience which are guaranteed under
s. 2
. I must
now proceed to discuss in more detail the various elements of the case.

Before doing so, I should set out certain provisions of the
Education Act ,
R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2
:

21(1) Unless excused under this section,

(a) every child who attains the age of six years on or before the first
school day in September in any year shall attend an elementary or secondary
school on every school day from the first school day in September in that year
until the child attains the age of sixteen years; and

(b) every child who attains the age of six years after the first school day
in September in any year shall attend an elementary or secondary school on
every school day from the first school day in September in the next succeeding
year until the last school day in June in the year in which the child attains
the age of sixteen years.

(2) A child is excused from attendance at school if,

(a) the child is receiving satisfactory instruction at home or elsewhere; .
. . . .

(5) The parent or guardian of a child who is required to attend school under
this section shall cause the child to attend school as required by this
section.

To state the obvious, these provisions make school attendance mandatory.
Without pursuing at tedious length the other provisions of the
Education Act
,
the obligation can be discharged, without direct cost to parents, by sending
children to the public or Roman Catholic separate schools, or by sending
children to independent schools. The latter involves tuition fees payable by
their parents.

V. THE SECTION 15 CLAIMS

The material portion of
s. 15
of the
Charter
reads as follows:

[bhEQUALITY RIGHTS

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to
the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and,
in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

The Adler applicants, the Elgersma applicants, and the OFIS which, as
intervener, supported their position, all alleged an infringement of the
s. 15

equality rights under the
Charter
. The arguments advanced on behalf of all
three have much in common, although there were individual differences of which
some note must be taken. Both the Adler applicants and the Elgersma applicants
sought a declaration of entitlement to funding by the province on a basis
equivalent to Roman Catholic separate schools and to public schools. OFIS did
not rely on the existence of public funding for Roman Catholic separate schools
in support of its argument. In my view and conclusion, funding of Roman
Catholic separate schools is not a relevant consideration in determining the
rights of these applicants. In view of that conclusion, I need not discuss the
position of the Roman Catholic schools in as much detail as would have been
necessary had that been a factor central to my disposition of the case. Some
comment, however, is necessary.

Prior to 1985, funding of Roman Catholic separate schools in Ontario was
provided only up to Grade 10. The constitutional validity of this restriction
was upheld by the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in
the case of Roman Catholic Separate School Trustees for Tiny v. The King ,

1928 CanLII 355 (UK JCPC)
, [1928] A.C. 363, [1928] 3 D.L.R. 753 sub nom. Tiny Separate School Trustees v.
The King . On July 4, 1985, the government of Ontario introduced Bill 30, the
Education Amendment Act, 1986 , S.O. 1986, c. 21, in the legislature, to extend
full public funding to Roman Catholic secondary schools. The day before the
introduction of this Bill, the Lieutenant Governor in Council referred to the
Ontario Court of Appeal the following constitutional question:

Is Bill 30, an Act to amend the Education Act, inconsistent with the
provisions of the Constitution of Canada including the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
and, if so, in what particular or particulars and in what
respect?

On the answer to this question the Court of Appeal divided: Reference re Act
to Amend the Education Act (1986),
1986 CanLII 2863 (ON CA)
, 53 O.R. (2d) 513, 23 C.R.R. 193 (Bill 30
Reference). Both the majority and the dissenting judgments assumed that the
Privy Council decision in Tiny was binding on them. The majority of the court
upheld the constitutional validity of Bill 30. The dissenting judgment held
that Bill 30 provides a discriminatory unequal benefit and for that reason it
is inconsistent with
s. 15(1)
. The dissenting opinion went on to hold that the infringement
of
s. 15
could not be justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

The Supreme Court of Canada unanimously upheld the constitutional validity
of Bill 30 [
1987 CanLII 65 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 1148, 36 C.R.R. 305]. The majority judgment
overruled the Privy Council decision in Tiny and held that funding of Roman
Catholic separate schools was guaranteed to Grade 13 by
s. 93(1)
of the

Constitution Act, 1867
. The concurring judgments found it unnecessary to
reconsider the Tiny case. The court unanimously held that Bill 30 was not
subject to, and therefore could not infringe, the
Charter
.

Both the Canadian Jewish Congress and OACSS intervened in the Court of
Appeal and in the Supreme Court of Canada and advanced arguments very similar
to those which were advanced on behalf of the applicants in this case. In
substance, the argument was that by providing Roman Catholics and Roman
Catholic schools with financial benefits not made equally available to other
taxpayers and other religious schools, Bill 30 violated the equality guarantee in

s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

On the hearing before me, the argument of counsel for the Attorney General,
and for the interveners supporting him, was that the constitutionality of Roman
Catholic funding had been laid to rest by the Bill 30 Reference and that the
arguments based on such funding had been determined and could not be pursued
anew in these proceedings.

Counsel for the applicants took the position that although the courts had
upheld the validity of Bill 30, and hence the constitutionality of Roman
Catholic school funding, the matters which were raised before me had not been
raised in the Bill 30 Reference and were open for decision in this case. The
argument was, first, that the issues raised before me had not been rendered res
judicata by the Bill 30 Reference. That submission I accept. The constitutional
reference, in its essential quality, does not involve a lis inter partes and
hence there is simply no technical base for the application of res judicata.
The argument was, further, that although the Bill 30 Reference had decided that
the rights of Roman Catholics to funding of their separate schools were immune
to
Charter
review in the sense that they could not, by or in the course of such
review, be abrogated or cut down, it was still open to consider the existence
of those rights as a reality and to determine against that reality whether the
denial of funding to the applicants and their schools was unconstitutional in
that the legislation was under-inclusive. I am not prepared to accept that legislation
which has been held to be a valid exercise of the provincial power to legislate
in matters pertaining to education should, at the same time, provide the
fulcrum for an argument that it is unconstitutional in its effect. The question
put to the court in the Bill 30 Reference was framed in terms such as to invite
full scrutiny under the Charter and the court dealt with it accordingly. In my
view and conclusion, the funding of Roman Catholic separate schools in Ontario
is a constitutional anomaly, with its roots in a historic political compromise
made as an incident of the Confederation of 1867. As such, I am not prepared to
give it any weight in the disposition of the issues which I must decide. I
reach that conclusion aware of what must be the popular view that the anomaly
represents inequality and a want of equity. This was fully recognized and dealt
with by the judges in the Supreme Court of Canada.

But the s. 15 argument does not end there. In the factum of the intervener,
OFIS, the issue is raised in these terms:

The State confers a substantial benefit upon persons whose religious beliefs
are consistent with the education provided in Ontario public schools, when it
provides education in those schools free of charge. When equivalent funding is
denied to persons who dissent from the public school curriculum on religious
grounds they are thereby deprived of equal benefit of the law on the basis of
their religious beliefs, contrary to
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

The response made by the Attorney General is that the public school system
does not discriminate on the basis of religion, and that once the funding of
Roman Catholic separate schools is removed from the analysis (as, in my view,
it should be), all religions in Ontario are treated equally: no private
religious schools receive direct public funding and no religion is given
preferential treatment within the public school system.

In its factum, OFIS relies on Andrews. v. Law Society of British Columbia ,

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143, 56 D.L.R. (4th) 1. In that case, the Supreme Court of
Canada struck down a provision of the Barristers and Solicitors Act, R.S.B.C.
1979, c. 26, which made Canadian citizenship a requirement for admission to the
bar of that province. In Andrews, McIntyre J., while in the result he was in
dissent, wrote on the application of s. 15 in terms which were accepted by the
majority. After reviewing cases and articles dealing with discrimination,
McIntyre J. summarizes the concept in these words, at p. 174 S.C.R., p. 18
D.L.R.:

I would say then that discrimination may be described as a distinction,
whether intentional or not but based on grounds relating to personal
characteristics of the individual or group, which has the effect of imposing
burdens, obligations, or disadvantages on such individual or group not imposed
upon others, or which withholds or limits access to opportunities, benefits,
and advantages available to other members of society.

This definition was quoted by Wilson J., writing for the court in R. v.
Turpin ,
1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1296, 39 C.R.R. 306, at pp. 1331-32 S.C.R., pp. 335-36
C.R.R. After doing so, she goes on to write:

In determining whether there is discrimination on grounds relating to the
personal characteristics of the individual or group, it is important to look not
only at the impugned legislation which has created a distinction that violates
the right to equality but also to the larger social, political and legal
context. McIntyre J. emphasized in Andrews (at p. 167):

For, as has been said, a bad law will not be saved merely because it
operates equally upon those to whom it has application. Nor will a law
necessarily be bad because it makes distinctions.

Accordingly, it is only by examining the larger context that a court can
determine whether differential treatment results in inequality or whether,
contrariwise, it would be identical treatment which would in the particular
context result in inequality or foster disadvantage. A finding that there is
discrimination will, I think, in most but perhaps not all cases, necessarily
entail a search for disadvantage that exists apart from and independent of the
particular legal distinction being challenged.

In R. v. Swain,
1991 CanLII 104 (SCC)
, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 933, 63 C.C.C. (3d) 481, Lamer C.J.C. sets
out the basic framework within which s. 15(1) claims may be analyzed. He states
at p. 992 S.C.R., pp. 520-21 C.C.C.:

The court must first determine whether the claimant has shown that one of
the four basic equality rights has been denied ( i.e., equality before the law,
equality under the law, equal protection of the law and equal benefit of the
law). This inquiry will focus largely on whether the law has drawn a
distinction (intentionally or otherwise) between the claimant and others, based
on personal characteristics. Next, the court must determine whether the denial
can be said to result in "discrimination". This second inquiry will
focus largely on whether the differential treatment has the effect of imposing
a burden, obligation or disadvantage not imposed upon others or of withholding
or limiting access to opportunities, benefits and advantages available to
others. Furthermore, in determining whether the claimant's
s. 15(1)
rights have
been infringed, the court must consider whether the personal characteristic in
question falls within the grounds enumerated in the section or within an
analogous ground, so as to ensure that the claim fits within the overall
purpose of s. 15; namely, to remedy or prevent discrimination against groups
subject to stereotyping, historical disadvantage and political and social
prejudice in Canadian society.

Dealing with the first portion of the test, it seems to me that a
distinction has been created by the
Education Act
and that this distinction
results in a violation of the applicants' right to equal benefit of the law.
Those (the majority) whose children attend the public schools receive the
benefit of an education for their children free of any direct costs
attributable to that education. Those whose children do not attend the public
schools, because their religious convictions prevent them from allowing their
children to do so, do not receive that benefit.

Looking to the second part of the test, the answer is less easy to discern.

On the one hand, it is possible to say of the applicants, and others
similarly situated, that they have been made subject to a distinction based on
grounds related to personal characteristics, namely, religious conviction,
which distinction has the effect of imposing "burdens, obligations or
disadvantages" not imposed upon others. On the other hand, it can be
argued that there are many schools outside the public school system which do
not owe their existence to religious conviction, that direct funding is not
provided to any schools outside the public school system, and therefore that the
distinction made is not based on religious conviction.

One must also have regard for what was said by Wilson J. in the portion of
her judgment in Turpin which is quoted above. I have regard in particular for
her concluding words:

A finding that there is discrimination will, I think, in most but perhaps
not all cases, necessarily entail a search for disadvantage that exists apart
from and independent of the particular legal distinction being challenged.

Looking at the larger context, and taking a historical perspective, it is
difficult for me to avoid the conclusion that there is here a distinction based
on religion. It may well be an ironical, unintentional, and indirect
consequence of the attempt to create a system of public education free from religious
bias. I do not think that changes the essential nature of the distinction.

In my view and conclusion, those whose religious and conscientious beliefs
do not permit them to attend the public schools do not receive equal benefit of
the law to which they are entitled under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

VI. THE SECTION 2 CLAIM

The material portion of
s. 2
of the
Charter
reads as follows:

Fundamental Freedoms

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a) freedom of conscience and religion;

(b) freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom of
the press and other media of communication;

(c) freedom of peaceful assembly; and

(d) freedom of association.

The applicants contend that the
Education Act
which makes attendance at
school mandatory, together with the non-funding of independent schools, is an
infringement of the guarantee of freedom of conscience and religion contained
in
s. 2
( a) of the
Charter
. Untutored by authority, I do not think I would have
arrived at that conclusion. Persons in the position of the applicants are at
liberty to act consistently with the dictates of their conscience and religion
and to meet the requirements of the Education Act by having their children
educated in other than the public schools. For that they must pay the costs of
tuition. However, I am persuaded by the authorities that my initial view would
be in error. I am led to my conclusion that there has been an infringement of
s. 2( a) chiefly by three cases: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R.
295, 13 C.R.R. 64; R. v. Edwards Books & Art Ltd.,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, 28
C.R.R. 1; Zylberberg v. Sudbury Board of Education (1988),
1988 CanLII 189 (ON CA)
, 65 O.R. (2d) 641, 34
C.R.R. 1 (C.A.).

In Big M the court declared to be unconstitutional a provision of the Lord's
Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13, requiring Sunday closing. The court held that
this was a breach of the freedom of religion of those who were required by
conscience and religion to observe a day of rest other than Sunday. In his
judgment in that case, Dickson J. discussed freedom of religion in the
following terms at pp. 336-37 S.C.R., p. 97 C.R.R.:

The essence of the concept of freedom of religion is the right to entertain
such religious beliefs as a person chooses, the right to declare religious
beliefs openly and without fear of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to
manifest religious belief by worship and practice or by teaching and
dissemination. But the concept means more than that.

Freedom can primarily be characterized by the absence of coercion or
constraint. If a person is compelled by the state or the will of another to a
course of action or inaction which he would not otherwise have chosen, he is
not acting of his own volition and he cannot be said to be truly free. One of
the major purposes of the
Charter
is to protect, within reason, from compulsion
or restraint. Coercion includes not only such blatant forms of compulsion as
direct commands to act or refrain from acting on pain of sanction, coercion
includes indirect forms of control which determine or limit alternative courses
of conduct available to others. Freedom in a broad sense embraces both the
absence of coercion and constraint, and the right to manifest beliefs and
practices.

(Emphasis added)

The court held that a law, religious in purpose, which denies non-Christians
the right to work on Sunday, denies them the right to practise their religion
and infringes their religious freedom.

In Edwards Books the court was concerned with whether a section of the
Retail Business Holidays Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 453, violated
s. 2
of the

Charter
. The court held that there was an interference with freedom of religion
in that Sunday closing legislation imposed a burden on those whose religious
observances required them to close on Saturday as well, but that it was
justifiable under
s. 1
of the Charter. At p. 759 S.C.R., p. 33 C.R.R., Chief
Justice Dickson, for the majority, writes:

It matters not, I believe, whether a coercive burden is direct or indirect,
intentional or unintentional, foreseeable or unforeseeable . All coercive
burdens on the exercise of religious beliefs are potentially within the ambit
of
s. 2
( a).

(Emphasis added)

In Zylberberg the court had to deal with provisions of the Education Act ,
R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, and a regulation passed under the Act providing for the
Lord's Prayer and scripture reading as opening exercises. Provision was made
for exemption from participation in religious exercises by children of persons
who objected to such exercises. The majority in the Divisional Court upheld the
regulation. The dissenting opinion found that the necessity to seek an
exemption was a potential source of embarrassment to the objector which
constituted an indirect form of pressure or coercion. The majority in the Court
of Appeal agreed with this dissenting opinion.

In argument, counsel for the Elgersma applicants asked that I make three
findings of fact. In my view, they bear on the topic I am now discussing.

1. That the Elgersma applicants, by reason of the dictates of religion, are
required to provide education for their children in accordance with the
principles of the Christian Reformed Church.

2. That the education necessary to these applicants to fulfil that
obligation is not available in the publicly funded schools.

3. That the individual applicants suffer a burden in securing for their
children education consistent with their religious beliefs.

I have neither hesitation nor doubt in making such findings. Indeed, counsel
for the Attorney General, in argument, did not resist the making of those
findings, but submitted that they led to no consequences which were material to
the case. I will deal with that submission shortly. Findings in very similar
terms are appropriate to the Adler applicants.

Counsel for the Attorney General sought to turn the force of these findings
by submitting that the
Charter
protected only against government action, and
that any burden or disadvantage, and any resultant pressure or coercion,
resulted not from government action, but from the religious beliefs of the
applicants, and from the practice of the independent schools of charging
tuition. Indeed, he submitted, it is at most government inaction (failing to
fund independent schools) which is at the root of the applicants' problems, and
there was no obligation on the government to provide such funding. That is a
respectable argument, but it seems to me to beg the question, and, in any
event, to be inconsistent with the results in Big M , Edwards and Zylberberg.
It is the legislation (government action) which makes school attendance
mandatory and the price of escape from that mandatory provision is the payment
of tuition fees by those parents who, by religious and conscientious belief,
are precluded from taking advantage of the publicly funded school system.

Realizing that analogies are never without hazard, the analogy to Zylberberg
is compelling. In that case, as in this, government action made mandatory a
course of conduct from which an exemption was provided, but the exercise of the
exemption involved a cost or burden. Indeed, it seems to me that in any of Big
M , Edwards, or Zylberberg, it could have been argued with as much force as in
the instant case that the burden or constraint was the consequence of religious
belief, and not of government action -- the impugned law. The judgment of Beetz
and McIntyre JJ., in Edwards, at p. 789 S.C.R., p. 57 C.R.R., reflects just
such an argument.

In my view and conclusion, the applicants' rights under
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
have been infringed. In the light of that conclusion I have not deemed
it necessary to deal with infringement of rights under
s. 2
(b) and ( d) of the
Charter as raised by counsel for OFIS.

Before leaving this topic, I should make some reference to R. v. Jones,

1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 284, 25 C.R.R. 63. That case involved consideration of
provisions of the
Alberta School Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. S-3
, which are similar to
the relevant provisions of the Education Act. The appellant refused to send his
children to public school and refused to seek an exemption in the manner
prescribed by the Alberta School Act. He was prosecuted under that Act. His
contention that there was an infringement of his religious freedom was rejected
on appeal, and in the Supreme Court of Canada, by the judges who dealt with the
application of
s. 2
( a) of the
Charter
. I have not found it easy to reconcile
some of the pronouncements in Jones with Big M, Edwards and Zylberberg. But I
have arrived at and stated my conclusions and wish only to make it clear that
Jones was not overlooked in the process.

VII. THE SECTION 7 CLAIM

Neither the Adler applicants nor the Elgersma applicants alleged any
infringement of s. 7. Such an infringement is alleged by the intervener, OFIS.
In view of my conclusions on the claims under ss. 2( a) and 15, I do not deem
it necessary to deal with the claim under s. 7. I have found infringements of

Charter
rights which would give grounds for relief if the legislation is not
saved by s. 1.

VIII. THE CASE ON SECTION 1

Section 1
of the
Charter
provides:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
guarantees the rights and
freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law
as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.

This is the aspect of the case which I have found to be the most difficult.
Before approaching the formula which is customary in the application of s. 1, I
propose to state my views of this aspect of the case in more general terms.
This will serve as background to my disposition of this aspect of the case and
to my application of the formula.

It is the position of the Attorney General, and of those interveners who
support him, that the government was charged with power and authority, and had
the duty, to legislate in matters relating to education. Historically, the
government dealt with the matter by the provision for public schools and Roman
Catholic separate schools. (I do not think the discussion needs to be
complicated by mention of the single Protestant separate school.) I have
already discussed the position of the Roman Catholic separate schools and shall
not deal with it further. The Attorney General, and those interveners who
support him, contend that the interest of the state in education, in a secular
pluralist society, is best served by the public education at present provided
in this province under the Education Act and under attack in these proceedings.
I do not need, for the moment at any rate, to trace in detail the history of
the religious component in the public school curricula. The limits of that
component were sharply curtailed by the decisions in Zylberberg and in Canadian
Civil Liberties Assn. v. Ontario (Minister of Education) (1990),
1990 CanLII 6881 (ON CA)
, 71 O.R. (2d)
341, 46 C.R.R. 316 (C.A.) (the Elgin County case). It is further the position
of the Attorney General that the funding of separate, religiously based schools
would place this public system in jeopardy.

The applicants and the interveners supporting them contest both these
positions. They submit that any preference for the public school system is, at
best, a matter of opinion. It is further the position of the applicants, and
the interveners supporting them, that there is no persuasive evidence that the
funding of the independent schools would place the public system in jeopardy.

The case has proceeded on the assumption that the limitations on the right
to equality and freedom of religion were "prescribed by law" in
accordance with
s. 1
of the
Charter
, and that s. 1 was therefore applicable,
and the arguments were focused on whether the respondents had shown that the
limitations were justified. The onus of proving that an infringement of a
Charter right constitutes a reasonable limit on that right, which can be
demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society, is on the party
seeking to maintain the status quo and uphold the infringement. In their factum
the Adler applicants address the burden resting on the respondents under s. 1
in the following terms:

To discharge their section 1 burden, the Respondents must:

(a) demonstrate on the basis of cogent and persuasive evidence that the
objectives in denying public funding to religious-based schools other than
Roman Catholic separate schools are of sufficient importance to warrant
overriding constitutionally protected rights in
sections 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the

Charter
; and

(b) satisfy the following three-fold proportionality test:

(i) the non-funding must be rationally connected to the achievement of the
government's objectives; it must not be arbitrary, unfair or based on
irrational considerations;

(ii) the government's failure to fund the Jewish day schools must impair as
little as possible the rights in question -- i.e. freedom of religion and
equality rights; and

(iii) there must be a proportionality between the effects of the non-funding
of the Jewish day schools and the objectives which have been identified as
having sufficient importance.

In the factum filed on behalf of the Elgersma applicants, the question is
addressed in these terms:

. . . in particular the Respondents must establish that:

1. the objective of not providing funding for Christian independent schools
must be of sufficient importance, in that it relates to concerns which are
pressing and substantial in a free and democratic society, to warrant
overriding the applicants' constitutionally protected rights and freedoms;

2. the means chosen to achieve that objective (ie. the total absence of
funding for Christian independent schools) must pass a proportionality test in
that the means must (a) be "rationally connected" to the objective
and not be arbitrary, unfair or based on irrational considerations, (b) impair
the right or freedom in question as "little as possible" and (c) be
such that their effects on the limitation of rights and freedoms are
proportional to the objective.

While it is not of critical importance to the disposition of the case, the
test as thus put by counsel appears to me argumentative and slightly distorted.
I say this without criticism. I realize that it is the non-funding of the
independent schools which is the focus of the applicants' case. In my view,
that focus is too narrow. Such non-funding is an incident, albeit an important
incident, of the whole school system put in place by the Education Act. It
seems to me that it is in this larger context that the non-funding of the
independent schools must be considered.

I take for guidance the following quotations from the judgment of Dickson
C.J.C. in R. v. Oakes,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, 19 C.R.R. 308 at pp. 136, 138-40,
139 S.C.R., pp. 335, 336-37 C.R.R.:

The rights and freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
are not, however,
absolute. It may become necessary to limit rights and freedoms in circumstances
where their exercise would be inimical to the realization of collective goals
of fundamental importance. For this reason, s. 1 provides criteria of
justification for limits on the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Charter.
These criteria impose a stringent standard of justification, especially when
understood in terms of the two contextual considerations discussed above,
namely, the violation of a constitutionally guaranteed right or freedom and the
fundamental principles of a free and democratic society. . . . . .

To establish that a limit is reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free
and democratic society, two central criteria must be satisfied. First, the
objective, which the measures responsible for a limit on a
Charter
right or
freedom are designed to serve, must be "of sufficient importance to warrant
overriding a constitutionally protected right or freedom": R. v. Big M
Drug Mart Ltd. , supra, at p. 352. The standard must be high in order to ensure
that objectives which are trivial or discordant with the principles integral to
a free and democratic society do not gain s. 1 protection. It is necessary, at
a minimum, that an objective relate to concerns which are pressing and
substantial in a free and democratic society before it can be characterized as
sufficiently important.

Second, once a sufficiently significant objective is recognized, then the
party invoking s. 1 must show that the means chosen are reasonable and
demonstrably justified. This involves "a form of proportionality
test": R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. , supra, at p. 352. Although the nature
of the proportionality test will vary depending on the circumstances, in each
case courts will be required to balance the interests of society with those of
individuals and groups. There are, in my view, three important components of a
proportionality test. First, the measures adopted must be carefully designed to
achieve the objective in question. They must not be arbitrary, unfair or based
on irrational considerations. In short, they must be rationally connected to
the objective. Second, the means, even if rationally connected to the objective
in this first sense, should impair "as little as possible" the right
or freedom in question: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd. , supra, at p. 352. Third,
there must be a proportionality between the effects of the measures which are
responsible for limiting the
Charter
right or freedom, and the objective which
has been identified as of "sufficient importance".

The first of the criteria to which attention is directed is the legislative
objective of the impugned legislation.

(1) Legislative objective

The factum filed on behalf of the Attorney General, in dealing with the
legislative objective does so in these terms:

These objectives include:

i) The provision of a tuition-free, secular, public education, universally
accessible to all Ontario residents without discrimination on the basis of
race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex or mental or physical
disability.

ii) The establishment of a public education system which fosters and
promotes the values of a pluralist, democratic society, including social
cohesion, religious tolerance and understanding.

iii) The establishment of democratically elected local boards of education,
accountable to the local electorate, to provide an element of local management
and control throughout Ontario.

iv) The establishment of an education funding mechanism which:

a) places a primary obligation on local boards to raise revenue for
education programs and services;

b) ensures that all public school boards have equitable financial resources
to provide a base level of education programs and services;

c) permits local school boards to devote additional resources in accordance
with local priorities.

The state has both authority and responsibility in education. The
legislature of Ontario has the plenary power under
s. 93
of the
Constitution
Act, 1867
to make laws in relation to education. The importance of a public
system of education was recognized by the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v.
Jones, supra. At p. 299 S.C.R., p. 74 C.R.R., in the judgment of La Forest J.,
we find the following:

No proof is required to show the importance of education in our society or
its significance to government. The legitimate, indeed compelling, interest of
the state in the education of the young is known and understood by all informed
citizens.

I do not consider it necessary to refer to evidence of, or to review in
detail, the history of education in this province in order to conclude that the
legislative objectives, as enunciated in the portion of the factum quoted
above, are sufficiently significant to meet the first test in Oakes. I think it
hardly open to question that the provision of a system of education is a "pressing
and substantial" necessity in a modern state.

(2) The means of accomplishing the objective

(a) Rational connection

It is when attention is directed to the means that the boot begins to pinch.
The means adopted by the government infringe the constitutional rights of the
applicants in the ways which I have previously discussed. It now has the onus
of demonstrating that those means which have that effect are rationally
connected to its legislative objectives. On this issue, the case for the
government, broadly stated, is that the current system of education is the most
appropriate response to its legislative obligations in the matter of education,
and that the exclusion of independent schools from public funding is a
necessary component of that system in that the funding of such independent
schools would be inimical to the welfare of the public schools. This is really
the nub of the case. The Attorney General, and the interveners supporting him,
advance persuasive opinions that the funding of independent schools would be
inimical to the public school system in many ways. It would have the result of
attracting to the independent schools an undetermined (and undeterminable)
number of students, including, perhaps, some of the brightest and best. It
would require the application of financial resources with unpredictable results
for the public school system.

This is countered by the applicants, first, on the ground that much of the
anticipated adverse effect is speculative; secondly, that various degrees of public
funding of independent schools exist elsewhere without disastrous consequences
for the public school system. They say further that fiscal considerations
should not enter into such a determination and quote Wilson J. in Singh v.
Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) ,
1985 CanLII 65 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177, 14
C.R.R. 13.

These are elusive issues. There is in the record a plethora of reports and
learned articles and assertions of opinion from which a respectable argument
could be made for either point of view. That being said, it seems to me that
little more need be said on this aspect of the case. I do not conceive the onus
on the respondents to be proof, on the balance of probabilities, that the means
of accomplishing the objective is the best means of doing so; only that the
means adopted represent a rational response to the problem. In 1984 the
government created a Commission on Private Schools in Ontario. The report of
that Commission (the Shapiro Report) is instructive in many ways, not least in
that it reflects the complexity of the problem and the diversity of views which
exist concerning its solution. One may agree or disagree with its conclusions
and recommendations. The government has not implemented its recommendations. I
have disagreed with its conclusions concerning
s. 15
of the
Charter
and the
funding of Roman Catholic separate schools. Both its existence and its content
are persuasive that the government has proceeded rationally in formulating its
policy.

It is not to be overlooked that among the imponderables which would attend
public funding of independent schools is the potential range of such schools
and the extent of the demand for such funding. There is already pending in this
court an application, of a nature similar to those which are now before me,
brought on behalf of other faith communities outside the Judeo-Christian
tradition.

Before leaving this aspect of the s. 1 analysis, I should comment on the
argument for the applicants that the potential adverse consequences, for the
public school system, of funding the independent schools are a matter of
speculation and that no firm evidence of such adverse consequences is before
the court. Junior counsel for the Elgersma applicants put the argument very
well. However, I did not understand her to argue that there was not any risk of
such consequences. The evidence would not support such a conclusion. In the
report of the Shapiro Commission and in the affidavit of Professor Lawton, and
the material there referred to, there is evidence that such a risk exists. It
is a legitimate concern to those charged with responsibility in educational
matters. The significance of the risk as a factor for consideration is not
eliminated simply because, in its nature, it is incapable of precise prediction
and measurement.

The decision not to fund the independent schools was rationally adopted with
a view to furthering the scheme of education put in place by the impugned
legislation. The decision may have been wrong (I do not imply that it was), but
it was not unsupported by evidence and it was not "arbitrary, unfair or
based on irrational considerations".

I do not accept the argument put forward in the supplementary factum of OFIS
that the government relies on "convenience and expediency" in
advancing its purpose. Faced with an obligation to create an educational system
to meet the needs of a pluralistic society, it created a system which it
conceived to be one that would best meet the needs of that society. It was a
task to daunt the bravest. The result is far from perfect. One would have to
lead a life more sheltered, even, than that ascribed to judges, not to know
that it has many frailties and is beset by many vicissitudes. But to impugn its
whole purpose and objective is, in my view, unsound. I do not see in it a
government purpose to make attendance at secular public schools mandatory. I
see in it a purpose to make education widely available on a non-sectarian
basis.

(b) Degree of impairment of right

The question which must here be asked and answered is whether the scheme
envisaged by the Education Act impairs "as little as possible" the
rights of freedom of religion and equality. It is difficult to see how the
objectives of the government as I have identified them could have been effected
with less impairment save by creating, as concomitant to the public school
system, a scheme of funding independent schools in the manner now sought in
these proceedings. Without the constitutional provisions which underlie funding
of Roman Catholic schools, the government might be restricted or precluded by
constitutional considerations from creating such a scheme. That is a question I
need not decide, but its existence is relevant to considering whether its
objectives could have been pursued with less impairment of the applicant's
rights. It should also be noted that the independent schools do receive some
limited, indirect, financial support. It takes the form of exemption from real
property taxes, income tax deduction for tuition attributable to religious
instruction, and income tax deductions for charitable donations.

Those who find themselves, by reason of religion or conscience, unable to
send their children to the public schools, need not do so if the children
receive satisfactory instruction elsewhere. Provision of that instruction is a
burden on their parents, but one which, in my view, cannot be readily avoided.
If a burden is coercive, it is nonetheless a burden, but it seems to me that in
considering and applying this portion of the s. 1 test, the nature of the burden,
although not determinative, is relevant. No one is compelled to attend the
public schools. No one is compelled to educate children in a manner
inconsistent with religious belief. No one is denied the right to educate
children in accordance with religious belief.

The legislature "is not required to search out and to adopt the
absolutely least intrusive means of achieving its objective": R. v.
Chaulk,
1990 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1303, 1 C.R.R. (2d) 1, at p. 1341 S.C.R., p. 27 C.R.R.

I conclude that the degree of impairment of the applicants' rights is within
permissible limits.

(c) Proportionality between effect of public school system and legislative
objectives

In pursuit of its objective, which I have already discussed, the government
chose to provide direct funding only for the public and Roman Catholic separate
schools. I have concluded that the impugned legislation is rationally connected
to that objective, and impairs the rights of the applicants as little as
possible. Are the means chosen to give effect to its objective proportionate to
the adverse effects on the applicants? This seems to me the most difficult
question to answer in the s. 1 analysis in this case. It may be that this
portion of the Oakes formula is less suited to this case than to some others. In
any event, I do not understand the Oakes test to be inflexible. In the judgment
of Chief Justice Dickson in Edwards, the following statement is found at pp.
768-69 S.C.R., p. 41 C.R.R.:

Both in articulating the standard of proof and in describing the criteria
comprising the proportionality requirement, the court has been careful to avoid
rigid and inflexible standards.

It seems to me that in this case the proportionality between objectives and
effects must be largely one of opinion, on which specific evidence could be
neither readily available nor of much assistance. In any situation where
conflicting interests arise between the majority and a minority, the resolution
of that conflict will almost inevitably inflict some disadvantage on the
minority. In the instant case the objective of a broadly based system of
secular public education is a complex and onerous undertaking. That some
elements of the population would be in some way and to some extent offended and
inconvenienced was almost inevitable. Having regard for these considerations,
the effects, in my view, were not out of proportion to the objective.

In my view and conclusion the respondents have satisfied the onus under
s. 1

of the
Charter
.

(3) Addendum on s. 1

In a case such as this, it is in considering the application of s. 1 that a
court is faced most directly with the need to determine the extent, if at all,
to which it is appropriate to intervene in the scheme of things as it has been
arranged by the legislature. That it should at times intervene is essential if
force and effect are to be given to the
Charter
. That it should at times
refrain from intervention is apparent from the provisions of s. 1. The nature
of the legislative scheme and of the problems which were involved in its
adoption are, in my view, relevant factors in deciding whether it is
appropriate to intervene or to defer to the legislature. In this case these
factors seem to me to militate against intervention. I have found that the
respondents have met the tests as outlined in Oakes. However, it is only proper
to acknowledge that throughout my deliberations I have been influenced by the
thought that I was considering, particularly in the case on s. 1, matters
better suited to consideration by the legislature. Perhaps the time has come
for the courts to enunciate something analogous to the "political
question" doctrine or the "public purpose" doctrine which have
evolved in the United States. I do not purport to do more than raise the
question. The answer must be provided at some other level in the judicial
hierarchy.

Earlier in these reasons, I have adverted to the hazards of taking
statements in judgments out of context. This is a vice in any field of law and
it seems particularly common and perhaps particularly pernicious in constitutional
matters. At the risk of falling foul of my own admonitions, I find some support
for my view that this is not a case for intervention in Reference re Public
Service Employee Relations Act (Alberta),
1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 313, 28 C.R.R. 305
sub nom. Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v. Alberta (Attorney General) ,
where Mr. Justice Le Dain, at p. 392 S.C.R., p. 384 C.R.R. (admittedly in
another context), writes:

The resulting necessity of applying
s. 1
of the
Charter
to a review of
particular legislation in this field demonstrates in my respectful opinion the
extent to which the court becomes involved in a review of legislative policy
for which it is really not fitted.

I include this quotation merely as giving evidence of judicial recognition
in the Supreme Court of Canada that there are some areas best left to the
legislature.

Counsel for both parties made reference to Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec
(Attorney General) ,
1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 927, 39 C.R.R. 193. I find helpful in my
present considerations some words of the Chief Justice appearing at p. 993
S.C.R., pp. 247-48 C.R.R. After quoting from Oakes, he writes:

Thus, in matching means to ends and asking whether rights or freedoms are
impaired as little as possible, a legislature mediating between the claims of
competing groups will be forced to strike a balance without the benefit of
absolute certainty concerning how that balance is best struck. . . . When
striking a balance between the claims of competing groups, the choice of means,
like the choice of ends, frequently will require an assessment of conflicting
scientific evidence and differing justified demands on scarce resources.
Democratic institutions are meant to let us all share in the responsibility for
these difficult choices.

In McKinney v. University of Guelph,
1990 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 229, 2 C.R.R. (2d) 1,
at pp. 304-05 S.C.R., p. 53 C.R.R., La Forest J. writes:

I turn then to the question whether mandatory retirement impairs the right
to equality without discrimination on the basis of age "as little as
possible". In undertaking this task, it is important again to remember
that the ramifications of mandatory retirement on the organization of the
workplace and its impact on society generally are not matters capable of
precise measurement, and the effect of its removal by judicial fiat is even
less certain. Decisions on such matters must inevitably be the product of a mix
of conjecture, fragmentary knowledge, general experience and knowledge of the
needs, aspirations and resources of society, and other components. They are
decisions of a kind where those engaged in the political and legislative
activities of Canadian democracy have evident advantages over members of the
judicial branch. . . .

When one looks at the impugned legislation, one finds nothing harsh,
oppressive, or intrusive. Indeed, it is difficult to see how the government
objective of a public system of education could have been given effect with a
lesser degree of interference. At most there has been a failure to meet, by
positive action, the educational needs of the applicants, as the applicants
perceive those needs to be.

I find myself much in sympathy with what was written for the court in
Reference re Education Act of Ontario and Minority Language Education Rights (1984),

1984 CanLII 1832 (ON CA)
, 47 O.R. (2d) 1, 11 C.R.R. 17 (C.A.), at p. 57 O.R., p. 71 C.R.R.:

The judiciary is not the sole guardian of the constitutional rights of
Canadians. Parliament and the provincial Legislatures are equally responsible
to ensure that the rights conferred by the
Charter
are upheld. Legislative
action in the important and complex field of education is much to be preferred
to judicial intervention.

(Emphasis added)

I also find myself in sympathy with what was said by the Supreme Court of
the United States in San Antonio Independent School District v. Rodriguez, 411
U.S. 1 (1973), at p. 43:

The ultimate wisdom as to these and related problems of education is not
likely to be divined for all time even by the scholars who now so earnestly
debate the issues. In such circumstances, the Judiciary is well advised to
refrain from imposing on the States inflexible constitutional restraints that
could circumscribe or handicap the continued research and experimentation so
vital to finding even partial solutions to educational problems and to keeping
abreast of ever changing conditions.

In the instant case, the court is asked to direct the government of Ontario
to embark on a new and radical method of financing education in this province,
and to do so when the means of implementing it have yet to be devised and its
effects are largely unpredictable and imponderable. It is asked to do so in the
face of numerous reports and learned articles from which no consensus is
readily discernible. I am much in sympathy with the position of the applicants.
There are few things which touch a concerned parent more closely than the
appropriate education of children. To feel oneself at a disadvantage in giving
effect to that concern produces a very real sense of grievance. Notwithstanding
my sympathy with the position of the applicants and with their sense of
grievance, I am in doubt that the court is the appropriate forum for relief.

IX. SCHOOL HEALTH SUPPORT SERVICES

Both the Adler application and the Elgersma application included claims with
respect to School Health Support Services. As already noted, the Adler
application includes a request for "an order that the Province of Ontario
extend school health support services to the children in the Jewish Day
Schools". The Elgersma application includes a request for

. . . a declaration that s. 1 of the Ontario Regulation 638/ 84 (s. 44a of
Reg. 452, R.R.O. 1980, as amended) made under the Health Insurance Act
infringes rights guaranteed under
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
by reason of its failure to provide school health support
services to students in OACSS member schools who require such services and an
order that the Province of Ontario extend school health support services to any
student enrolled in an OACSS member school who requires such services . . .

(1) The facts

Matan Kezwer, the son of the applicant Paul Kezwer, has a hearing
impairment. According to the affidavit of Paula Kezwer, he needs some special
attention to overcome his hearing difficulties, and possibly some speech
therapy in order to bring his communication skills up to the level of his
peers.

Walter Elgersma is the son of the applicant, Leo Elgersma and his wife
Alice. He was born with spina bifida and hydrocephalus. According to the
affidavit of Leo Elgersma, Walter required medical services, including
catheterization and physical therapy, as well as transportation daily from home
to the school.

Joel Pott is the youngest son of the applicant, Harry Pott. According to the
affidavit filed by his father, he is a non- verbal, developmentally handicapped
child with many autistic tendencies and a number of behavioural problems, and
his needs are such that he often requires one on one guidance.

(2) Standing

In the factum filed on behalf of the Attorney General, it is submitted that
of the applicants only Leo Elgersma has standing to maintain this portion of
the application, because neither Paula Kezwer nor Harry Pott have provided
evidence that their children are directly affected by the legislation in
question. In my view, all of the applicants who have raised this issue should
be accorded standing.

I arrive at this conclusion based on two cases. The first of these is Canada
(Minister of Justice) v. Borowski ,
1981 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1981] 2 S.C.R. 575, 64 C.C.C. (2d) 97.
Borowski, a prominent crusader against abortion, sought a declaration that a
section of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, relating to procurement of
miscarriage was invalid and inoperative as infringing upon rights guaranteed by
the Constitution. After discussing earlier cases dealing with status, Martland
J., writing for the majority, wrote as follows at p. 598 S.C.R., p. 115 C.C.C.:

I interpret these cases as deciding that to establish status as a plaintiff
in a suit seeking a declaration that legislation is invalid, if there is a
serious issue as to its invalidity, a person need only to show that he is
affected by it directly or that he has a genuine interest as a citizen in the
validity of the legislation and that there is no other reasonable and effective
manner in which the issue may be brought before the Court. In my opinion, the
respondent has met this test and should be permitted to proceed with his
action.

The second case is Finlay v. Canada (Minister of Finance),
1986 CanLII 6 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R.
607, 33 D.L.R. (4th) 321. Finlay sued for a declaration that certain payments
out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada were illegal on the ground that
they were not made in accordance with the applicable statutory authority. He
was held not to have a sufficiently direct personal interest in the legality of
the payments to bring him within the general requirement for standing to sue.
It was held, however, that he should be granted standing as a matter of
judicial discretion. I think the proper conclusion to be drawn from these cases
is that if a serious question is raised as to the validity of legislation,
particularly where its constitutionality is called in question, the court has a
broad discretion to grant standing so that the matter may be brought before the
court.

(3) The statutory framework

The impugned legislation is in Reg. 452 of R.R.O. 1980 [under the Health
Insurance Act , R.S.O. 1980, c. 197]. The material portions are in the
following terms:

44a(1) In this section,

(a) "home care facility" means a home care facility as defined in
clause 44(1)( a);

(b) "school" means a school as defined in paragraph 49 of
subsection 1(1) of the Education Act;

(c) "school health support services" means,

(i) the services that are provided, on a visitation basis, by a nurse,
physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist or nutritionist,

(ii) the training, supervision or consultation services of a nurse,
physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist or nutritionist to support
personnel referred to in paragraph 64 of subsection 1(1) of the Education Act ,
and

(iii) the provision of dressings and medical supplies necessary for the
services referred to in subclause (i),

but does not include an item referred to in subclause (i), (ii) or (iii)
where the item is being provided by Hotel Dieu Hospital, Kingston, Chedoke-
McMaster Hospitals or Laurentian Hospital or a rehabilitation centre or
crippled children's centre listed in Schedule 10;

(d) "special education program" means a special education program
as defined in paragraph 63 of subsection 1(1) of the Education Act; . . . . .

(2) School health support services provided by a home care facility to an
insured person who is placed in a special education program in a school are
prescribed as insured services.

The definition of "school" as contained in para. 49 of s. 1(1) of
the Education Act , R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, is as follows:

49. "school" means,

i. the body of public school pupils or separate school pupils or secondary school
pupils that is organized as a unit for educational purposes under the
jurisdiction of the appropriate board, or

ii. the body of pupils enrolled in any of the elementary or secondary school
courses of study in an educational institution operated by the Government of
Ontario,

and includes the teachers and other staff members associated with such unit
or institution and the lands and premises used in connection therewith . . .

The definition of "special education program" is in these terms:

63. "special education program" means, in respect of an
exceptional pupil, an educational program that is based on and modified by the
results of continuous assessment and evaluation and that includes a plan
containing specific objectives and an outline of educational services that
meets the needs of the exceptional pupil;

Home care facilities are defined in the regulation as follows:

44(1) In this section,

(a) "home care facility" means,

(i) a local board of health of a municipality or a health unit, or

(ii) an agency,

approved by the Minister to provide home care services;

(4) Resolution of the issue

The applicants' complaint is that "school health support services"
are provided only for schools as defined in the Education Act. Independent
schools do not fall within that definition and do not receive such services.
Thus, it is said, the applicants' rights under
s. 15(1)
, to equal benefit of
the law, are infringed, as are their rights under
s. 2
( a).

It is first necessary to characterize the issue. If it is fundamentally one
of health services, then different considerations apply from those which have
been discussed in the foregoing portions of these reasons. If, however, the
issue should be characterized as one of educational services, then similar if
not identical considerations apply. In my view, the latter is the correct
characterization. It is not, I think, in issue that, simply qua health
services, such services are available to the children of the applicants as they
are to any other children in the province. It is the delivery of these services
in the school setting which is the bone of contention. Slightly different
considerations may apply to special transportation facilities, but these seem
to me to fall clearly within the scope of educational services.

Viewed as educational services, I see no reason why the various health care
benefits should be viewed in any different light than any other of the range of
services which are involved in the educational process.

If I am correct in that conclusion, then I see no reason why this portion of
the applications requires treatment different from those with which I have
already dealt. There appear to me to be the same infringements of
s. 15
and
s.
2
of the
Charter
and the same considerations with respect to the application of
s. 1. I would dispose of the applicants' claim to relief on these matters as on
the others with which I have already dealt.

X. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS

In the result, I have concluded that the applicants' rights under s. 15 and

s. 2
( a) of the
Charter
have been infringed, but that the impugned legislation
is saved by s. 1. Both applications shall be dismissed. I should not think it
was a case for costs and none are ordered. However, no argument was heard on
the subject and if any party wishes to contend for a different disposition, the
matter may be spoken to on an appointment arranged for the purpose.

At the conclusion of the oral argument, I expressed my appreciation to
counsel for the manner in which these proceedings were conducted throughout.
The adherence of so many parties to a pre-arranged schedule leading to the
hearing cannot have been accomplished without a large measure of co- operation
between counsel. The arguments throughout were articulate and competent. The
arrangement of the material was admirable. The writing of a judgment is a
solitary endeavour. In its pursuit, when counsel are not available to answer
the questions which the judge should have asked during argument, the
organization of the material is of utmost importance. For all of the efforts of
counsel I am most grateful.
